young.html: John Dewey was an American teacher of teachers. He spent his long life asking: what makes a lesson really teach you something?

Dewey said every experience teaches you something, but not always something good. If you are bored stiff in class, you might learn that learning is boring! A good experience is one that makes you want to know more and helps you do more next time. He called that growth.

young.html: A growing project. Pick something to make together: a pancake breakfast, a bird feeder, a family newspaper. Along the way, notice what new questions come up (How much flour for twice as many people? Which birds came?). Write them down. Those questions are what Dewey meant by growth.

full.html: John Dewey (1859–1952) was a philosopher, a founder of pragmatism with Peirce and James, and the most famous American writer on education. In 1896 he opened a Laboratory School at the University of Chicago to test his ideas, and in 1916 he published Democracy and Education. By the 1930s a "progressive education" movement claimed him as its leader. Experience and Education (1938), a short book from a lecture series, is partly his warning to that movement.
No excerpts here. The book was published in 1938 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. Library editions are easy to find.

Dewey describes two camps. Traditional education passes down a fixed body of knowledge and rules from above: textbooks, drills, silent rows of desks. Progressive education begins from the child's interests and activity. Dewey criticizes the first for imposing material that has little to do with students' lives. But he criticizes many progressives just as sharply: rejecting the old ways, he says, is not a philosophy. Freedom without direction, and activity without thought, can be as empty as drill.

full.text: Two tests of a good experience

full.html: The heart of the book is a theory of experience with two principles:

head: Principle
Dewey's idea (our summary)
rows: Every experience takes something from those before it and changes those that come after. A good one opens the way to further growth; a bad one closes it, for example by making a student bored, careless or afraid.
Every experience is a meeting between the learner (needs, abilities, past experience) and the outer situation (materials, people, setting). The teacher's job is to arrange situations that fit both.

full.html: An experience can be lively and still be mis-educative if it leads nowhere or builds bad habits. Dewey also points to collateral learning: the attitudes students pick up alongside the lesson, such as a love of reading or a dislike of it, which may last far longer than the facts.

Dewey compares a good classroom to a game. In a game, the rules are not felt as a boss's orders; they are part of the activity, and the group keeps them. So in a good school, order comes mainly from shared work, not from the teacher's will alone. The freedom that matters most is freedom of intelligence: the power to form purposes and judge how to reach them, not merely to move about. The teacher is not a bystander: because he or she has more experience, the teacher must plan, select materials and guide, and organized subject matter, science, history, mathematics, should grow out of experience into ordered knowledge.

Dewey's ideas shaped American schooling for much of the century, from project work and hands-on science to the idea that schools should prepare citizens for democracy. They have always been argued over. Critics on one side blamed "progressive" schools for weak teaching of basic skills and knowledge; Dewey's defenders reply that this book already criticizes exactly that. Others, such as the educator E. D. Hirsch, have argued that children need a large shared core of knowledge to think well, and that progressive methods can widen gaps between students. Research on learning today supports some of Dewey's points, for example the value of active practice and of building on what students already know, while also finding that beginners often learn best from clear, guided instruction.
Thinking Dewey said children should do whatever they like. This book argues the opposite: experience must be chosen and guided, and the teacher carries real responsibility.

items: Plato's Republic and Rousseau's Emile both made education the key to a good society; Dewey ties it to democracy.
James's Pragmatism, an earlier rung, judged ideas by their working; Dewey judges experiences by where they lead.
Locke wrote that the mind is shaped by experience; Dewey added that experience is an active meeting of person and world.
The site's Memory Ladder looks at what research says about practice and review, a modern conversation about how learning lasts.
What makes an experience educational rather than just fun, or just hard?
How much should children choose what they learn?
What is the teacher for, if students learn by doing?
Why might a school matter for a democracy?

questions: Think of the best lesson you ever had. Did it pass Dewey's two tests?
What is something you learned "on the side" (an attitude or habit) without anyone teaching it?
Are rules in a game different from rules made by a boss? How?
Dewey criticized both old-style and new-style schools. What would you keep from each?
What new questions did your last project lead you to?
